html:
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also called the Iroquois or the Six Nations, is a union of Iroquoian peoples in what is now New York State and southern Ontario and Quebec. It was founded some time before European contact and still exists today.

The name means "people of the longhouse", after the long bark houses where related families lived together. The five founding nations, from east to west, were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. The Tuscarora joined in 1722, making six.

Oral tradition tells how the Peacemaker and Hiawatha, with Jigonhsasee, ended a time of feuds by bringing the nations under the Great Law of Peace. Chiefs from each nation met in a council at Onondaga, and clan mothers chose and could remove the chiefs. The founding date is much debated: one reading of the tradition gives 1142, while many scholars prefer about 1450 to 1600.

With guns from the fur trade, the Confederacy grew strong in the 1600s. In the Beaver Wars it scattered or absorbed many neighbouring peoples. Around 1700 its power reached from the Great Lakes to the Ohio valley, and for nearly two centuries it played the French, Dutch and British against one another.

The American Revolutionary War split the Confederacy, and many who sided with Britain moved to Canada (see Loyalists to Canada). Some Americans, including Benjamin Franklin, admired its union, and the US Congress later recognised its influence on the Constitution, a claim historians still discuss. The Confederacy keeps its council and has issued its own passports.
